Bloody
blŭd´y
adj. (stained with blood, guilty of bloodshed; rendering Hebrew dam in construct, ish damim)
From blood, Anglo-Saxon blod. The Hebrew idiom is man of bloods — the plural marking not one killing but a character formed by them.

Biblical Definition

Bloody in the Authorized Version is a moral verdict, not a description of a stain. The Hebrew phrase behind it is man of bloods, and the psalmist prays plainly, “the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” (Psa 5:6) — bloodiness and deceit paired, as they were in the devil who was a murderer and a liar from the beginning. David asks not to be gathered with them (Psa 26:9), and warns that “bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days” (Psa 55:23). The word cuts close: Shimei hurls it at David himself — “Come out, come out, thou bloody man” (2Sa 16:7) — and David does not answer the charge, because it was not wholly false. The strangest use is Zipporah's at the inn, casting the foreskin at Moses' feet: “Surely a bloody husband art thou to me” (Exo 4:25) — a covenant kept by blood at the last possible moment, and Moses' life spared by it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bloody as stained with blood, and then as cruel, murderous, given to the shedding of blood, or having a cruel savage disposition.

expand to see more

BLOOD´Y, a. Stained with blood; as a bloody garment.

2. Cruel; murderous; given to the shedding of blood; or having a cruel savage disposition; applied to animals.

3. Attended with bloodshed; marked by cruelty; as a bloody battle.

Bloody-minded, having a cruel, ferocious disposition; barbarous.

Key Scripture

Psa 5:6 — "Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man."

Psa 55:23 — "But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee."

2Sa 16:7 — "And thus said Shimei when he cursed, Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial:"

Exo 4:25 — "Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me."

Modern Corruption

Bloodshed made entertainment and abstracted by distance, while the church grows squeamish about the blood Scripture insists upon — a culture at ease with violence and uneasy with atonement.

expand to see more

The inversion is precise and worth naming. Simulated bloodshed is consumed for pleasure at a scale no previous age could have imagined, and real bloodshed is rendered tolerable by distance and euphemism. Meanwhile the same culture — and much of the church with it — finds the blood of the cross distasteful, and hymnody about a fountain filled with blood is quietly retired as primitive. Scripture holds the exact opposite valuation: bloodshed by man is abhorred, and blood shed by God's appointment is the only thing that cleanses.

Exodus 4:25 is the passage that keeps this entry from becoming abstract. On the way to deliver Israel, Moses is met by God and nearly killed over an uncircumcised son, and Zipporah saves him with a flint and a word: a bloody husband art thou to me. It is a scene that resists sentimentality about covenant. God is in earnest about the sign He appointed, and the deliverer of Israel is not exempt from it. Blood was required then, and blood is required still — which is why the gospel is not squeamish.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dam (H1818), blood; the idiom ish damim, a man of bloods, marking a settled character; chatan damim (Exo 4:25), a bridegroom or husband of blood.

expand to see more

Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; in the plural damim it denotes bloodguilt, the blood that cries from the ground (Gen 4:10).

Hebrew ish damim — a man of bloods; the abhorred figure of Psa 5:6 and Psa 55:23, and Shimei's charge against David (2Sa 16:7).

Hebrew chatan damim — a husband of blood; Zipporah's startling phrase at the inn, tying marriage, covenant, and circumcision together (Exo 4:25).

Usage

"“The LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” — bloodshed and lying always travel together."

"“Come out, come out, thou bloody man” — and David did not answer it."

"“Surely a bloody husband art thou to me” — the covenant kept at the last moment."
